title: 9 Best Manifestation Apps in 2026, Honestly Compared
description: The best manifestation apps in 2026, honestly compared: Kaizen, I am, ThinkUp, Innertune, Gratitude, 5 Minute Journal, Vision Board Perfectly Happy, Day One and Anicca, checked against US App Store listings in November 2026.
markdown:
By Anicca · November 2026

Updated November 2026

**A disclosure before anything else:** we make Anicca, one of the apps on this list. You should read every word below knowing that. We have tried to earn your trust the only way a maker can, by giving every other app its real strengths, giving our own app its real limits, and telling you plainly when a different app will suit you better. Anicca is added ninth here, scored with the same six questions as every other app, and we do not rank it first.

We checked each app's App Store listing, Google Play listing or official website before describing it, and we only describe features we could confirm there. The comparison this page follows checked its listings in October 2026; we re-checked the US App Store listings on 19 November 2026 through Apple's public listing data and note the current US rating and rating count in each section. We left out prices for other apps because they change often and vary by country. Before you subscribe to anything, including Anicca, open the store page and read the in-app purchase list yourself. For the wider affirmation field compared by what each app lets you do with the words, see our [full guide to the best affirmation apps](https://aniccaai.com/blog/best-affirmation-apps-2026-11-05), and for the daily version of the same practice, see our [guide to the best daily affirmation apps](https://aniccaai.com/blog/best-daily-affirmation-apps-2026-11-18).

## How we compared them

Almost every manifestation app is built around one main practice, so rather than scoring apps on a single scale, we asked six questions of each one. We ignored star ratings, which tell you an app is liked, not whether it fits how you practice.

1. **What is the core practice?** Reading affirmations, listening to them, recording your own, scripting, gratitude journaling or vision boards.

2. **How personal is the content?** A shared library that everyone sees, a library you can add to, or content written from what you tell the app.

3. **How much friction is there on a tired day?** An app you only open when you feel motivated is a hobby, not a habit. We looked at how short a useful session can be.

4. **How does it treat a missed day?** Streaks motivate some people and quietly push others away. We noted which apps use them.

5. **What can you do for free?** Some apps have a real free version, some have a trial, and some keep most features behind a subscription.

6. **What happens to your private material?** Journal entries and voice recordings are some of the most personal data you will ever put in an app.

## Quick comparison

| App | Best for | Core practice | Platforms | Free option |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Innertune | Listening during the day and at night | Affirmation audio over music and beats | iPhone, Android | Free listening; premium adds own-voice recording |
| Gratitude | Journaling, affirmations and vision boards in one place | Gratitude journal with prompts | iPhone, iPad, Android | Free to download; Pro subscription |
| 5 Minute Journal | A short, structured gratitude habit | Guided morning and evening entries | iPhone, Android | Free core journal; premium extras |
| Vision Board Perfectly Happy | Building a visual board | Photo vision boards with affirmations | iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch | Free to download; subscription |

Platforms and free options as listed on each app's store page or official site in October 2026, following the comparison this page follows, with US App Store listings re-checked on 19 November 2026. “Free option” describes what is available without paying, not the full feature set. Check the store page in your country before subscribing.

## Kaizen: best for personalized manifestation

**What it is:** a manifestation practice spread across the day. In the morning you get affirmations written from your own journal — your goals, your doubts and your recent wins — instead of a stock library. In the evening there is a guided manifestation story set in an ordinary day of the life you are building, which you can have read aloud or read along with, followed by a journal prompt, a gratitude entry and a release practice where you name a limiting belief and drag it into a flame. At night you get a message of under a minute from a year-from-now future self. On the US App Store it is listed as Kaizen: Manifestation App (version 1.4.3, updated 17 November 2026, free to download, 1 US rating at 1.0 stars on 19 November 2026 — a very new listing, so treat that count as a snapshot of a new app, not a track record).

**Standout features:** lock screen and home screen widgets put your affirmation where you already look, so the practice does not depend on remembering to open the app. The night message is read in a warm library voice, or, only if you opt in, in a private clone of your own voice that is never shared or sold, can be deleted in one tap, and is removed within about 24 hours. There is also a voice studio for recording affirmations in your own voice, a sound library with solfeggio frequencies and binaural beats, a library of guided stories sorted by life goal, and small anonymous community circles matched by the path you are on. The growth page shows days in, entries written and your longest streak, and missing a day never comes with a guilt message.

**Trade-offs:** Kaizen is a paid membership. After a 3-day free trial it costs $19.99 a month or $199.99 a year, which is more than several apps on this list. Journaling, crisis resources, data export and account deletion stay free, but the practice itself does not. It is also built around a guided routine, so if you want a free library of quotes and nothing more, or a blank page with no prompts, a lighter app will suit you better and cost less.

**Best for:** people who want the practice to feel written for them, and who like being walked through a short morning, evening and night routine rather than assembling one themselves.

## I am: best for affirmations you don't have to open an app for

**What it is:** I am, from Monkey Taps, puts affirmations where you already look. Its App Store listing describes affirmations on your lock screen (a new one every day), home screen widgets with a focus you choose, and reminders delivered through the day on a schedule you set. It runs on iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch, and its Google Play listing notes Wear OS support. US App Store, 19 November 2026: 4.8 stars from 739,613 ratings, version 7.10.0, updated 18 November 2026 — by far the largest rating base on this page.

**Standout features:** the effort required is close to zero. You pick intentions such as self-esteem or confidence, set reminder frequency, save favorites, and the sentences find you. It is one of the most widely used apps in the category.

**Trade-offs:** the free version is ad-supported, and premium is a separate purchase. The core experience is short sentences from a shared library, so there is no journaling, scripting or guided audio. For some people that simplicity is the whole appeal.

**Best for:** people who want gentle reminders woven into the day, and anyone who has bounced off apps that ask for ten minutes of focused time.

## ThinkUp: best for recording affirmations in your own voice

**What it is:** ThinkUp, from Precise Wellness, is built around a simple idea: you record affirmations in your own voice and listen back to them over background music. Its listing frames the app as a 28-day program for building a daily affirmation habit. It is available on iPhone and Android. US App Store, 19 November 2026: ThinkUp-Daily Affirmations app, 4.7 stars from 7,522 ratings, version 1.18.11.

**Standout features:** a library of over 300 affirmations across more than ten life goals (self-esteem, stress relief and career among them), the option to write your own, an image on each affirmation card, daily reminders, and, on iPhone, logging your listening time to Apple Health as mindful minutes.

**Trade-offs:** the free version lets you record only a few affirmations with one default music track. Longer recordings, unlimited affirmations and music changes are part of premium. The app focuses on single-sentence affirmations, so if you want longer stories, prompts or a journal, you will need a second tool.

**Best for:** people who already know what they want to say and want to hear it in their own voice on a commute or a walk.

## Innertune: best for listening, day and night

**What it is:** Innertune, from Innertune Media, plays affirmations over music or beats. Its App Store listing says it builds a playlist for your situation, and you can match the audio to beats for focus, relaxation or sleep. The official site links to both the App Store and Google Play. US App Store, 19 November 2026: Innertune: Daily Affirmations, 4.8 stars from 12,142 ratings, version 6.14.3, updated 5 November 2026.

**Standout features:** the free tier is generous for listening: unlimited listening time, a night mode and daily reminders. Premium adds AI-personalized playlists, a larger choice of narrator voices, more beats, offline downloads and recording affirmations in your own voice. The listing describes a library of tens of thousands of affirmations and hundreds of playlists.

**Trade-offs:** passive listening is easy to keep up but also easy to tune out. Recording in your own voice needs the subscription, and recent versions add streaks and a 21-day plan.

**Best for:** people who would rather listen than read or write, especially at bedtime. If sleep problems or anxiety have lasted weeks, an app is a fine wind-down tool, but please also talk to a doctor; persistent insomnia and anxiety are very treatable.

## Gratitude: best for journaling, affirmations and vision boards in one app

**What it is:** Gratitude: Self-Care Journal, from Hapjoy, starts with a daily gratitude journal and adds the other pieces many manifestation routines use. It is available on iPhone, iPad and Android. US App Store, 19 November 2026: 4.9 stars from 44,994 ratings, version 6.0.3, updated 7 November 2026.

**Standout features:** journal entries can include photos and voice recordings, with hundreds of prompts and daily reminders. There is an affirmations section where you can read or listen to a library or write your own and add music or your voice. Vision boards are built from sections and goal ideas with photos, quotes and affirmations, and the app can turn a board into a short video set to music. A Daily Zen feed adds quotes and short articles.

**Trade-offs:** with this many sections, it can take a few days to find the parts you actually use. The listing does not spell out which features need the Pro subscription, so check the paywall. It also uses streaks.

**Best for:** people who want gratitude at the center, with vision boards and affirmations close by.

## 5 Minute Journal: best for a short, structured gratitude habit

**What it is:** the app version of Intelligent Change's paper Five Minute Journal. It gives you a guided flow for a morning entry and an evening entry based on gratitude and reflection. It is on iPhone and Android. US App Store, 19 November 2026: 5 Minute Journal・Daily Diary, 4.8 stars from 17,630 ratings, version 4.3.31, updated 9 November 2026.

**Standout features:** the free version is a complete journal: guided morning and evening entries, daily quotes, weekly challenges, reminders, a calendar view, a passcode or Face ID lock, and export to PDF, HTML or Dropbox. Premium adds photos and video, custom questions, a mood tracker, a look-back feature and a home screen widget.

**Trade-offs:** it is a gratitude journal, not a manifestation app, so there are no affirmations, audio or scripting templates. The structure is fixed unless you pay for custom questions. It also shows streaks.

**Best for:** starting with the habit that has the best research behind it, or anyone who likes the paper version.

## Vision Board Perfectly Happy: best for building a visual board

**What it is:** a vision board app from Perfectly Happy Meditation, available on iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch. The comparison this page follows could not confirm an Android version. US App Store, 19 November 2026: Vision Board Perfectly Happy, 4.8 stars from 4,606 ratings, version 2.2.288.

**Standout features:** you build a board from your own photos or from built-in image libraries, and the app can turn it into a video. It also includes a library of thousands of affirmations and quotes that can be read aloud, home screen widgets, a gratitude journal, a mood tracker, background music and daily reminders to look at your board.

**Trade-offs:** if images do not move you, most of its value goes unused. Full access is by subscription.

**Best for:** visual thinkers who used to cut pictures out of magazines and want a board they can see on their phone every day.

## Anicca: best for a short card on a hard day, with no streaks

**What it is:** Anicca (ours) is an iPhone affirmation app built for difficult days rather than for building a board or a journal. You choose what you are struggling with during setup, enable notifications, and receive short cards to read. Its product page is titled “Free Daily Affirmations App for iPhone, No Streaks”, and that no-streaks point is deliberate: a missed day is not treated as a failure. US App Store, 19 November 2026: Daily Affirmations - Anicca, 5.0 stars from 1 rating, version 1.10.0, updated 18 November 2026, free to download, iOS 16.6 or later. That rating count is one — it is not comparable to the established apps above, and we say so plainly. The product page is at [aniccaai.com/affirmation-app](https://aniccaai.com/affirmation-app).

**Standout features:** the whole practice is one short card. There is no library to assemble, no board to build and no session to complete: choose your topics, allow a reminder, read a short card. Example cards on the product page include “You can be a work in progress and still speak to yourself with kindness” and “Rest does not need to be earned. You can let today be enough.”

**Trade-offs:** Anicca is iPhone only, with no Android, no journal, no vision board, no own-voice recording and no audio sessions. Anicca Premium is $59.99 per year in the US with a 3-day free trial, which is a real price for a deliberately small app; the free download is the way to test whether a short card is enough for you. Its rating base is a single rating, so there is no social proof to lean on yet.

**Best for:** people whose inner critic gets loud on hard days, who have been pushed away by streaks and guilt mechanics, and who want the lowest-friction version of the practice: one short, kinder thought that finds them.

## Looking for an app called “Manifest”?

Search “Manifest” in either store and you will find several apps with near-identical names (“Manifest,” “Manifested,” “Manifest - Daily Affirmations”) from unrelated developers. When the comparison this page follows checked in October 2026, each had relatively few ratings, and their features ranged from affirmation libraries to scripting exercises. Because we could not verify a single established app by that name, we left them out of the ranking.

If someone recommended “the Manifest app,” ask for the developer name and check it on the store page before you download.

### For scripting, a good journal often beats a manifestation app

Scripting means writing about your life as if your goal has already happened. All it really needs is a calm place to write that you trust. A general journaling app such as Day One works well: it is free to start, runs on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Android and the web, supports photos and audio, and its site describes end-to-end encryption and passcode or biometric locks. US App Store, 19 November 2026: Day One: Daily Journal & Diary, 4.8 stars from 119,014 ratings, version 2026.23, updated 10 November 2026. Your phone's notes app works too.

What you lose with a blank editor is guidance. Here is a short template you can paste into any journal app so the page is never empty:

Scripting template for any journal app

Date: one year from today.

Where I woke up this morning, and what I could hear:

The first thing I did that past me would be surprised by:

A conversation I had today that went well:

How my body felt at 3 p.m.:

One thing I did today that made this life possible:

The last line matters most: it turns a daydream into a clue about your next step.

## The best app by what you need

- **Content written for you, not a shared library:** Kaizen writes affirmations, stories and future-self messages from your own journal. Innertune's premium tier builds AI-personalized playlists if you prefer to listen.

- **Affirmations in your own voice:** ThinkUp is built entirely around this. Innertune (premium), Gratitude and Kaizen's voice studio also let you record yourself.

- **Scripting and long-form writing:** Day One or another private journal, with the template above.

- **Gratitude first:** 5 Minute Journal for a fixed, quick structure; Gratitude if you want prompts, photos and voice entries.

- **Vision boards:** Vision Board Perfectly Happy if the board is the point; Gratitude if you want a board alongside a journal.

- **Listening and sleep:** Innertune for affirmation audio over music. Kaizen's night message and sound library cover a shorter version of this.

- **Something free:** I am, 5 Minute Journal and Innertune all have free versions you can use daily. The 3-6-9 method needs nothing but paper.

- **Almost no effort:** Kaizen and I am both put affirmations on your lock screen and home screen widgets without opening anything. I am is the lighter, free-to-download option; Kaizen adds the journal-based practice.

- **A hard day, with no streak to break:** Anicca (ours) sends one short card chosen by what you are struggling with, and a missed day is not counted against you.

## What to look for in any manifestation app

### Personalization that fits, not just your first name

Generic affirmations can backfire for some people. In a well-known study, Wood, Perunovic and Lee (2009) asked university students to repeat “I'm a lovable person.” Those who already had high self-esteem felt slightly better, while those with low self-esteem felt worse than students who did not repeat it. A statement that clashes with what you believe can feel like an argument you are losing.

So look for an app that lets you edit, write your own, or soften statements into something believable. “I am becoming someone who saves a little every month” often lands better than “Money flows to me effortlessly.”

It also helps to know that in psychology research, “self-affirmation” usually means something different from repeating slogans: it means reflecting on values that matter to you. Cohen and Sherman (2014) reviewed this work and found that brief values reflection can reduce defensiveness under stress in many settings. An app that asks what matters to you, and not only what you want, is closer to that research.

### Low friction on bad days

The real test of a habit app is a Tuesday when you are tired. Check whether a useful session can take 60 seconds, whether you can do it in bed with the lights off, and whether you can skip a part without the app treating the session as failed.

### How it handles missed days

Streaks work well for some people. For others, a broken 40-day streak becomes the reason they quietly stop. Look at what the app shows you after a missed day. A neutral “welcome back” is fine. A red zero, a lost badge or a notification that implies you have let yourself down is a guilt mechanic, and it is worth noticing how it makes you feel.

### A plan, not only a picture

Be a little cautious about apps that offer only dreamy imagery. Kappes and Oettingen (2011) found that people who imagined an idealized future showed lower energy afterwards, measured by blood pressure and self-report, than people who imagined more realistic or mixed futures. Pleasant images can feel like progress without being it.

By contrast, a meta-analysis of 94 studies by Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006) found that “if-then” plans (for example, “If it is 8 a.m. on Monday, then I send one job application”) had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals. The best apps nudge you from feeling to acting, with a prompt about your next small step.

### Privacy for journals and voice recordings

Your journal may hold your money worries, relationship doubts and health fears. Voice recordings, and especially voice clones, are biometric data. Before you write anything personal, find the privacy policy and look for clear answers to these questions:

1. Are my journal entries sold or shared with advertisers or data brokers?

2. Are my entries or recordings used to train AI models, and if so, can I opt out?

3. Does the app show ads, and do ad partners receive any data about me?

4. If the app clones my voice, is that opt-in, where is it stored, and how fast is it deleted when I ask?

5. Can I export everything I have written, in a format I can open elsewhere?

6. Can I delete my account and data from inside the app, without emailing anyone?

7. Is there a passcode or biometric lock for the journal itself?

If a policy is vague on these points, assume the less private answer.

### Pricing you can actually see

Before you tap “start trial,” check the price after the trial, whether it bills monthly or yearly, and which features you keep if you cancel. The App Store lists every plan under “In-App Purchases.”

## Red flags to watch for

- **Promises of certain results.** Any app that tells you it will bring you money, a partner or a cure if you just listen enough is selling something no app can deliver. Affirmations and visualization can shape attention, mood and behavior. They cannot move events directly, and an honest app will not say otherwise.

- **Science claims with no sources.** Phrases like “rewire your subconscious” or a precise percentage of reality your brain “filters out” deserve a citation. If there isn't one, treat it as marketing.

- **Hidden or confusing plans.** A long list of weekly, monthly, yearly and “special” plans makes it hard to know what you are agreeing to. Weekly billing in particular adds up fast.

- **Cancellation that takes effort.** On iPhone and Android, subscriptions bought in the app can be cancelled from your device's subscription settings. An app that tells you to email support to cancel an in-app subscription is not being straight with you.

- **Pressure through fear.** Countdown timers on discounts, or language that blames you for “blocking” what you want. A good practice should leave you calmer.

- **Unclear handling of your voice.** If an app records or clones your voice and does not say clearly how to delete it, don't use that feature.

One kind note: if you are using an app to cope with debt, a breakup, low mood or health worries, it can be a comfort, but a doctor, a therapist or a nonprofit financial counselor can do things no app can.

## How to test an app properly in a 7-day trial

Most trials last three to seven days, enough to learn a lot if you test on purpose. Set a reminder to cancel a day before the trial ends, then follow this plan.

1. **Day 1: set it up honestly.** Give the app your real goals, not the polished version. Note how long setup takes and whether you saw the price before starting.

2. **Day 2: use it at your real time.** Open it when you would actually practice (on the bus, before coffee, in bed), not when you happen to be curious.

3. **Day 3: try the minimum.** Do the shortest useful session the app allows. If even that feels like a chore, that is useful information.

4. **Day 4: skip a day on purpose.** See what the app does when you come back. Notice whether you feel welcomed or scolded.

5. **Day 5: test the personal parts.** Write or record something of your own. Is it easy? Does the app use what you gave it?

6. **Day 6: check your data.** Find the export and delete options in settings. Read the privacy policy section on journals, recordings and AI training.

7. **Day 7: take one action.** Did the app prompt even one concrete step toward your goal this week? Decide, then cancel or keep before the renewal date.

Seven-day scorecard (copy into your notes)

Days I opened it without being reminded: __ / 7

Shortest useful session: __ minutes

Felt written for me (1 to 5): __

How it handled my missed day: welcoming / neutral / guilt-trippy

Export and delete easy to find: yes / no

One action it helped me take: __________

Price after trial, and billing: __________

Keep or cancel: __________

The most telling number is the first. An app you opened on four or more days without a nudge is probably one you will keep using.

## Using an app alongside a paper practice

Many people do best with both: an app for audio, reminders and personalization, and paper for slowing down. Give each tool one job so you aren't doing the same practice twice.

### A combination that works for many people

- **Morning, on your phone (2 minutes):** read or listen to your affirmations from an app, ideally ones you have edited until they feel believable.

- **Evening, on paper (5 minutes):** write three specific things you are grateful for, then one sentence of future-self journaling and one small step for tomorrow.

- **Weekly, on paper (15 minutes):** a longer script, or a page reviewing what actually happened this week.

The paper parts are where the research is strongest. Emmons and McCullough (2003) found that people who kept short gratitude lists reported higher well-being than people who listed hassles. King (2001) found that students who spent 20 minutes on each of four days writing about their best possible future self reported better mood afterwards, and visited the health center less often in the following months. Neither needs an app, though an app can make the reminder easier.

### If you keep forgetting one half

Anchor it to something you already do. “After I plug in my phone at night, I open my notebook” is easier to keep than “I will journal in the evening.” If the paper half still keeps slipping, move it into the app for a few weeks and bring paper back later.

## Questions

**What is the best manifestation app in 2026?**

The best manifestation app is the one that matches how you practice. Kaizen suits people who want personalized, guided manifestation with lock screen and home screen widgets; I am suits a simple widget library; ThinkUp suits own-voice affirmations; Innertune suits listening; and Gratitude or 5 Minute Journal suit a gratitude-first habit. Test one for a week before paying.

**What is the best free manifestation app?**

I am, 5 Minute Journal and Innertune all have free versions you can use every day. I am's free version is ad-supported, 5 Minute Journal's free journal includes morning and evening entries, and Innertune's free tier includes unlimited listening. Paper and a pen remain the cheapest manifestation tool of all.

**What is the best affirmation app?**

Kaizen puts affirmations written from your own journal on lock screen and home screen widgets, so it covers reading with no effort and personalization in one app. I am is the simpler, free-to-download widget option. For hearing them in your own voice, ThinkUp is built for exactly that. Anicca (ours) is the smallest option: one short card, chosen by topic, with no streaks.

**Is there a good law of attraction app?**

Yes, though most good ones describe themselves as affirmation, journaling or vision board apps rather than law of attraction apps. Choose by practice: affirmations, scripting, gratitude or visualization. Be cautious with any app that promises the law of attraction will bring you specific results.

**Do manifestation apps actually work?**

Manifestation apps work best as habit tools, not as a way to change events with thoughts alone. Research supports some of the underlying practices, such as gratitude journaling, writing about your best possible future self, and making specific if-then plans. The app's job is to make those practices easy to repeat.

**Is Kaizen free?**

Kaizen is a paid membership with a 3-day free trial, then $19.99 a month or $199.99 a year. Journaling, crisis resources, data export and account deletion are always free. If you want a free daily practice, one of the free apps on this page or a paper journal may suit you better.

**Which manifestation app lets me record my own voice?**

ThinkUp is built entirely around recording affirmations in your own voice. Innertune offers own-voice recording in its premium tier, Gratitude lets you add your voice to affirmations, and Kaizen has a voice studio plus an optional private voice clone for its nightly future-self message.

**Are manifestation apps safe for my privacy?**

They can be, but you should check each app's privacy policy before writing anything personal. Look for clear answers on whether entries are sold, shared with advertisers or used to train AI, and whether you can export and delete your data from inside the app. If a policy is vague, assume the less private answer.

**Is there a good vision board app?**

Vision Board Perfectly Happy is built specifically for vision boards on iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch, with your own photos or built-in images. Gratitude also includes vision boards alongside its journal and works on Android. Both can turn a board into a short video.

**Should I use more than one manifestation app?**

Usually not. Most people do better with one daily practice they repeat than several they dip into. If you combine tools, give each one a different job, such as an app for morning affirmations and a paper notebook for evening gratitude.

**How do I cancel a manifestation app subscription?**

Cancel through your phone's subscription settings, not by deleting the app. On iPhone, go to Settings, tap your name, then Subscriptions; on Android, open Google Play, tap your profile, then Payments and subscriptions. Cancel at least a day before a trial ends to avoid being charged.

**Is Anicca a manifestation app?**

Anicca is an affirmation app for hard days, not a full manifestation toolkit: it has no vision board, journal or scripting. If your practice is one short, kinder thought that finds you by notification — chosen from the topics you are struggling with, with no streak to break — it fits. If you want boards, journals or own-voice audio, choose one of the apps above instead. Anicca is free to download; Anicca Premium is $59.99 per year in the US with a 3-day free trial.
